items.foco: Chronic arterial hypertension as the main cause
items.title: Chronic arterial hypertension as the main cause
items.contentHtml:
Chronic arterial hypertension as the main cause

  • Chronic arterial hypertension (sustained blood pressure >140/90 mmHg for years) induces arteriolar vascular remodeling due to mechanical stress and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, being the most common cause of ischemic nephropathy in people over 50 years of age.
  • Kidney damage is correlated with the duration and severity of hypertension, not with the cause of hypertension; the absence of nephrotic proteinuria (less than 1 g/day) differentiates glomerulonephritis.
  • Chronic arterial hypertension precedes the deterioration of glomerular filtration; The diagnosis requires evidence of hypertension prior to the onset of kidney disease.

items.title: Afferent arteriolar injury with hyalinosis
items.contentHtml:
Afferent arteriolar lesion with hyalinosis

  • Afferent arteriolar hyalinosis is the characteristic histological lesion: hyaline eosinophilic deposition (plasma proteins and collagen) in the wall of the afferent arteriole, secondary to plasma extravasation due to hypertensive endothelial damage.
  • This finding is indistinguishable from that observed in diabetic nephropathy. mellitus, but in chronic arterial hypertension hyalinosis predominantly affects the afferent arteriole, while in diabetes it also affects the efferent arteriole.
  • Hyalinosis reduces the arteriolar lumen, generating downstream glomerular ischemia and activation of the intrarenal renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

items.title: Glomerular ischemia and focal sclerosis
items.contentHtml:
Glomerular ischemia and focal sclerosis

  • Glomerular ischemia secondary to afferent arteriolar hyalinosis produces collapse of the capillary tangle, thickening of the basement membrane and finally focal and segmental glomerular sclerosis (collapsing-type lesion).
  • The sclerosis is initially focal (only some glomeruli) and segmental (part of the tangle), progressing to global sclerosis over time; This distribution is key to differentiating from diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis.
  • In advanced stages, glomerular sclerosis is accompanied by tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis, correlating with the loss of the glomerular filtration rate.

items.title: Diffuse tubular and interstitial atrophy
items.contentHtml:
Diffuse tubular and interstitial atrophy

  • Diffuse tubular and interstitial atrophy is a late histological finding: the proximal convoluted tubules lose their brush border, flatten, and the interstitium shows fibrosis with mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate.
  • The extent of diffuse tubular and interstitial atrophy correlates better with glomerular filtration rate and progression to end-stage renal disease than isolated glomerular sclerosis.
  • In hypertensive nephropathy, diffuse tubular and interstitial atrophy is patchy and more marked in the renal cortex, unlike diabetic nephropathy, where there is diffuse interstitial fibrosis with Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules.

items.title: Non-nephrotic proteinuria (less than 1 g/day)
items.contentHtml:
Non-nephrotic proteinuria (less than 1 g/day)

  • Non-nephrotic proteinuria (less than 1 g/day) is typical of hypertensive nephropathy; exceeding 1 g/day suggests primary glomerulonephritis or nephropathy due to diabetes.
  • Proteinuria is usually low molecular weight (albumin and tubular proteins) due to tubulo-interstitial damage; In ENARM/MIR/EUNACOM type tests, they ask: the presence of proteinuria >3.5 g/day rules out hypertensive nephropathy as the sole cause.
  • Microalbuminuria (30-300 mg/day) may be the first sign of hypertensive kidney damage and predicts progression to end-stage renal disease.

items.title: Progressive increase in serum creatinine
items.contentHtml:
Progressive increase in serum creatinine

  • The progressive increase in serum creatinine reflects the slow loss of functioning nephrons, with a rate of decline in the estimated glomerular filtration rate of 2-5 ml/min/1.73 m² per year without treatment.
  • In early stages, serum creatinine may be normal; Early diagnosis requires calculating the estimated glomerular filtration rate using the CKD-EPI equation (Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration).
  • An acute increase in serum creatinine (>0.3 mg/dl in 48 hours) in a hypertensive patient should alert to accelerated nephrosclerosis or malignant hypertension, with arteriolar fibrinoid necrosis.

items.foco: Kidney ultrasound with asymmetry and decrease in size
items.title: Kidney ultrasound with asymmetry and decrease in size
items.contentHtml:
Renal ultrasound with asymmetry and decrease in size

  • The renal ultrasound with asymmetry and decrease in size shows small kidneys (<9 cm in length), with diffuse cortical thinning and increased echogenicity, reflecting fibrosis and loss of parenchyma.
  • Asymmetry >1.5 cm between both kidneys suggests renovascular disease (renal artery stenosis) rather than nephropathy primary hypertensive disease, which is usually bilateral and symmetrical.
  • In hypertensive nephropathy, renal ultrasound with asymmetry and decrease in size is a late finding; The absence of hydronephrosis, cysts or masses helps in the differential diagnosis with other causes of chronic kidney disease.

items.title: Differentiation with diabetic nephropathy
items.contentHtml:
Differentiation with diabetic nephropathy

  • Diabetes nephropathy presents with nephrotic proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), diabetic retinopathy (present in >90% of cases) and Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules in the biopsy; Hypertensive nephropathy has non-nephrotic proteinuria (less than 1 g/day) and absence of retinopathy.
  • In nephropathy due to diabetes, arteriolar hyalinosis affects both afferent and efferent, while in hypertensive nephropathy it is only afferent; renal ultrasound in diabetes shows kidneys of normal size or enlarged until advanced stages, not small from the beginning.
  • The presence of long-standing diabetes mellitus (>10 years) with neuropathy and retinopathy supports nephropathy due to diabetes; Chronic arterial hypertension without diabetes or significant proteinuria suggests hypertensive nephropathy.

items.title: Strict blood pressure control (lower goal 130/80)
items.contentHtml:
Strict blood pressure control (lower goal 130/80)

  • The goal of strict blood pressure control (lower 130/80 mmHg) in hypertensive nephropathy reduces the progression of end-stage renal disease and cardiovascular events, according to KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) 2021 guidelines.
  • Values below 120/70 mmHg should be avoided in patients with stage 4-5 chronic kidney disease due to the risk of renal hypoperfusion and worsening of the glomerular filtration rate.
  • Strict control of blood pressure (less than 130/80 mmHg) requires ambulatory blood pressure monitoring and stepwise pharmacological adjustment, prioritizing blockade of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

items.foco: Use of ACEI or ARA II as first line
items.title: Use of ACEI or ARA II as first line
items.contentHtml:
Use of ACE inhibitors or ARBs as first line

  • The use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors) or angiotensin II receptor antagonists (ARBs) as first line reduces proteinuria and slows the deterioration of the glomerular filtration rate, independently of the decrease in blood pressure.
  • In patients with serum creatinine >3 mg/dl or serum potassium >5.5 mEq/L, ACEI/ARBs are contraindicated; It is recommended to start with low doses and titrate every 2-4 weeks.
  • The combination of ACEI and ARB is not recommended due to the increased risk of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury without additional benefit in proteinuria or progression to end-stage renal disease.

items.title: Dietary sodium restriction
items.contentHtml:
Dietary sodium restriction

  • Dietary sodium restriction (<2 g/day, equivalent to <5 g of salt) enhances the antiproteinuric and antihypertensive effect of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin II receptor antagonists, reducing systolic blood pressure by 5-10 mmHg.
  • In disease Chronic kidney disease stage 3-5, sodium restriction in the diet (<2 g/day) helps control volume overload and resistant hypertension, but must be individualized to avoid hyponatremia or malnutrition.
  • High sodium intake (>4 g/day) nullifies the renoprotective effect of ACEI/ARBs, increasing proteinuria and accelerating the progression to end-stage renal disease.

items.foco: Risk of end-stage kidney disease without treatment
items.title: Risk of end-stage kidney disease without treatment
items.contentHtml:
Risk of end-stage kidney disease without treatment

  • Without blood pressure control, the risk of end-stage kidney disease (glomerular filtration rate <15 ml/min/1.73 m²) increases by 20-30% over 10 years in patients with established hypertensive nephropathy, especially if proteinuria >0.5 g/day coexists.
  • Progression to kidney disease End-stage renal disease is faster in uncontrolled chronic arterial hypertension (blood pressure >160/100 mmHg) and in the presence of obesity, dyslipidemia or smoking, which accelerate glomerular sclerosis.
  • The risk of end-stage renal disease without treatment is reduced by 50% with strict control of blood pressure (less than 130/80 mmHg) and the use of ACEI/ARBs as first line, according to reference studies such as the AASK (African American Study of Kidney Disease and Hypertension).
